items.title: AI Anxiety, Familiarity and Privacy Concerns: The Mediating Role of AI Literacy and the Moderating Role of Technophobia
items.abstract: This study examines how AI anxiety and familiarity relate to privacy concerns through AI literacy, and whether technophobia moderates the literacy–privacy relationship. Using survey data from 3,000 generative AI users in China and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we find that both familiarity and, contrary to expectations, anxiety are positively associated with AI literacy. AI literacy, in turn, is associated with greater privacy concerns and mediates both relationships, suggesting that increased knowledge may heighten awareness of data risks. Technophobia weakens the positive association between AI literacy and privacy concerns, although more technophobic users report higher overall concern. Exploratory age-group analyses suggest that the positive anxiety–literacy association is especially apparent among users in their 40s. These findings reveal a privacy awareness paradox and highlight the value of AI education that combines technical understanding, privacy awareness, and attention to users’ emotional responses.

items.title: AI Integration of Multi-omics Data for Drug Target Prediction in Glioblastoma
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with marked molecular and cellular heterogeneity, and current treatment provides limited long-term disease control. Single-target therapies have frequently failed because tumor subpopulations can differ in signaling dependencies, adapt under treatment pressure, and interact with a complex microenvironment. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate multi-omics data to improve drug-target prediction in GBM. It summarizes the pathological and molecular basis of GBM, evaluates current therapeutic targets and their limitations, and compares genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial, proteomic, metabolomic, and imaging data used for target discovery. Machine-learning, deep-learning, and network-based approaches are discussed with examples of multimodal risk stratification and candidate-target identification. The review also evaluates CRISPR screening as a functional validation step that can distinguish statistical associations from genuine tumor dependencies. Overall, AI-integrated multi-omics can provide a more context-specific approach to target prioritization by linking candidate genes to patient subgroups, cell states, and pathway activity. However, small cohorts, missing data, batch effects, limited model generalizability, and insufficient experimental validation remain major barriers. Future studies should combine larger multi-centre datasets with longitudinal and spatial profiling, interpretable models, functional perturbation, and prospective validation to support clinically translatable precision therapy in GBM.

items.title: AI Resources in Higher Education: What Instructors Need and How We Deliver
items.abstract: Abstract As generative AI reshapes higher education, instructors across the globe have become increasingly interested in integrating AI into the classroom, but they require trusted, timely, and relevant resources for such integration. To enable the development of an open educational resource (OER) that could be remixed and adapted to different teaching contexts and support inclusive access, this study examined what instructors want and need from an open resource on AI in teaching and learning in higher education and documented a process for developing professional development resources in a time of rapid technological change. This study employed a multiphase mixed-methods design. First, a statewide needs assessment survey was conducted with 149 instructors to identify needs, challenges, and priorities across diverse institutional and disciplinary contexts. Participants prioritized three core content domains for the resource—AI literacy, pedagogical strategies, and ethics—and favored interactive, adaptable, and open resources grounded in practical classroom applications. These findings were used to develop an OER prototype, on which 75 instructors provided feedback, affirming the utility of the resource and suggesting areas for further refinement. This study contributes an educator-informed process for translating instructors’ needs into the design and formative evaluation of an adaptable, openly licensed faculty development resource. This evidence-based, educator-driven approach demonstrates how those tasked with faculty development on AI can develop and refine timely resources that meet the needs of educators from diverse contexts, offering a flexible, scalable, and community-oriented pathway for bridging institutional resource gaps and advancing inclusive faculty development in the age of AI.

items.title: AI-Assisted Business Analysis: Usability, Trust Cues, and Human Oversight in Responses to Under-Specified Requests
items.abstract: Analysts increasingly turn to generative AI assistants for business-analysis work, yet they often start with short prompts that carry no organizational context. We examined how three general-purpose assistants respond to such under-specified requests and what their responses imply for usability, trust and human oversight. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini each received five prompts that named only a common business-analysis task: requirements analysis, requirements prioritization, user-story generation, stakeholder-needs analysis and business-process improvement. Each prompt was run three times per system in fresh sessions on 24 and 25 September 2026, giving 45 outputs, which we coded for accuracy, completeness, internal consistency, usability, transparency and support for human oversight. ChatGPT and Gemini explained the named concept in all 30 of their outputs and never asked about the user's situation. Claude asked a clarifying question in 13 of its 15 outputs, and five of its outputs contained little or no task content. Gemini covered 59 of 60 checklist elements but accounted for five of the six accuracy issues. No output expressed uncertainty or suggested verification, and every substantive output was generic. The results point to a trade-off between immediate completeness and handing control back to the analyst. They support a workflow in which analysts supply context, check outputs and validate them with stakeholders before acting on them.

items.title: AI-Based College Transportation Management
items.abstract: Colleges that run their own buses usually plan transport using fixed routes and estimated student counts. In practice, the number of students who actually travel changes from day to day, so some buses run with many empty seats while others are overcrowded. This paper presents the design of the AI-Based College Transportation Decision Support System, a full-stack web application that collects daily travel confirmations from students and uses rule-based software agents to analyse route-wise demand, check route compatibility, recommend bus allocation, and suggest seat optimization within capacity limits. Every recommendation is accompanied by a plain-language explanation, and no change becomes final until the administrator approves it. The previous allocation stays in force until a replacement plan is approved. The system is built with React.js, Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB, with JWT-based authentication and role-based access control. It uses predefined rules and calculations only; it does not use machine learning, GPS tracking, or external generative AI services. This paper describes the problem, the system architecture, the database design, the rule-based algorithms, and an illustrative worked example. Experimental evaluation on real college data is identified as future work.

items.title: AI-Driven multimodal sensing and secure data frameworks for next-generation biomedical wearable health monitoring systems
items.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), and wireless body area networks (WBANs) has introduced promising opportunities for continuous biomedical health monitoring. However, translating these technologies into robust wearable platforms requires overcoming challenges across intelligent multimodal diagnosis, edge-efficient processing, and end-to-end privacy preservation. This paper presents the AI-Driven Multimodal Secure Health Monitoring Architecture (AIMSHA), a four-tier framework structured across body sensor, edge gateway, fog aggregation, and secure cloud layers. AIMSHA couples multi-biosignal interpretation (EEG, EMG, ECG, and photoplethysmography) with explainable AI (XAI) transparency dashboards and lightweight hierarchical federated learning (FL). To protect distributed model updates against inference vulnerabilities, differential privacy noise perturbation is paired with attribute-based encryption (ABE) access controls and secure aggregation. Furthermore, a lightweight edge intrusion detection system mitigates malicious packet injection, while a permissioned blockchain ledger provides tamper-resistant provenance tracking for global model checkpoints and consent authorisations. Extensive evaluations across six task-aligned physiological benchmark cohorts demonstrate that the underlying MediFuse-DL backbone achieves a mean diagnostic Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.974. AIMSHA achieves a 41.3% reduction in communication overhead compared to centralized transmission baselines, maintains continuous sensor-tier monitoring autonomy exceeding 72 hours, and satisfies formal differential privacy guarantees ( $$\epsilon = 1.97$$ , $$\delta = 10^{-5}$$ ) over 100 federated communication rounds. Finally, we analyze software-as-a-medical-device regulatory considerations and clinical translation pathways, positioning AIMSHA as a viable preclinical baseline for secure, privacy-preserving remote patient monitoring. items.title: AI‐Driven Personalized Recommendations and Real‐Time Monitoring for the Prevention and Management of Obesity: Clinical Trial Protocol for the Multicentre BETTER4All Personalized Intervention
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity arises from complex interactions among genetic, biological, behavioral, and environmental factors. Traditional "one-size-fits-all" interventions often yield modest, short-term outcomes, failing to account inter-individual variability. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), polygenic risk scores (PRS), and digital health technologies now enable personalized and adaptive lifestyle interventions. OBJECTIVE: This paper presents the design and evaluation framework of the BETTER4All personalized intervention, a multicentre randomized controlled trial within the EU-funded BETTER4U project. The trial aims to integrate biological and behavioral data into tailored obesity prevention and management strategies. METHODS: . Participants will be randomized to an intervention group receiving AI and PRS-based lifestyle recommendations via a smartphone application, wearable device, and structured counseling, or to a control group receiving standard hypocaloric diet and lifestyle advice. The primary outcome is change in BMI at 6 months. Secondary outcomes include weight-loss maintenance at 1 year, metabolomic and gut microbiota biomarkers, lifestyle behaviors, and psychosocial parameters. Process evaluation incorporates measures of fidelity, acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness, alongside adherence metrics from the digital tools. CONCLUSION: The BETTER4All trial will provide evidence on the effectiveness and scalability of AI-driven, biologically informed personalization in obesity care, offering a methodological framework for integrating multimodal digital data, from omics and biomarkers to behavior and lifestyle, contributing to the advancement of precision public health strategies. items.title: Aligning Large Language Models for Safety in African Languages: A Case Study of Hausa
items.abstract: Safety alignment research for large language models (LLMs) remains concentrated on high-resource languages, leaving open how existing alignment methods perform in low-resource, culturally distinct settings. We study this question for Hausa, a language spoken by more than 200 million people across West Africa. We introduce HausaSafeLM, one of the first Hausa safety preference dataset, built from 10,000 prompts derived from PKU-SafeRLHF: 3,000 human-corrected (gold) and 7,000 machine-translated (silver) examples spanning six harm macro-categories. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and SFT followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) under both data regimes, evaluating on 500 harmful and 200 benign Hausa prompts.We find that the untuned base model appears highly safe by refusal-rate metrics alone, but this reflects limited Hausa generation ability rather than genuine alignment: its refusals are almost uniformly low quality. SFT improves both refusal fluency and precision and benefits substantially from the larger, noisier silver-tier data, while DPO sharpens refusal precision but comes at a steep, largely data-invariant cost to linguistic quality. No single configuration jointly maximizes safety, helpfulness, and fluency. Our results suggest that current alignment techniques teach models when to refuse more readily than how to do so fluently in underrepresented languages, and that refusal-rate metrics alone are an unreliable signal of safety in low-resource settings.

items.title: An AI/generative AI-assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates: a quasi-experimental study of attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce. Methods A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy. Results In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 ( P < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 ( P = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47; P < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21; P < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group ( P = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group ( P < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43; P < 0.001). Conclusions AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.

items.title: An evidence-gated strategy for translating targeted oncologic PET radiopharmaceuticals from molecular design to clinical use
items.abstract: Targeted oncologic positron emission tomography (PET) radiopharmaceutical development is often presented as a linear progression from target discovery to clinical imaging. Translation instead depends on interdependent biological, chemical, pharmacokinetic, manufacturing, and regulatory decisions. This Review examines those decisions as an integrated design problem. We consider how target accessibility and heterogeneity, vector format, linker and chelator chemistry, radionuclide properties, and whole-body pharmacokinetics jointly determine image contrast and normal-organ exposure. We then assess how radiosynthesis, analytical validation, molar activity, automation, and batch release determine whether a promising construct can become a reproducible clinical product. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) and somatostatin receptor platforms show how molecular imaging can support patient selection for radionuclide therapy when the diagnostic agent, therapeutic construct, trial population, and regulatory indication are aligned. By contrast, fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeted and other emerging platforms show why biodistribution or early human feasibility cannot establish clinical benefit. Across these examples, affinity alone is an insufficient design objective. The relevant endpoint is a clinically usable exposure profile that preserves target uptake while limiting background retention and dose to critical organs. Major unresolved issues include inconsistent head-to-head evaluation, incomplete dosimetry, product-specific manufacturing constraints, heterogeneous evidence standards, and region-dependent regulatory indications. We propose an evidence-gated framework that separates target suitability, molecular exposure, manufacturability, human performance, and implementation. This framework distinguishes established practice from early investigation and identifies studies most likely to reduce translational uncertainty.

items.title: API-TAIL: Detecting Model Substitution in LLM APIs through Temperature-Aligned Likelihood Tails
items.abstract: Commercial language model APIs return only text, allowing a provider to cut costs by quietly routing a fraction of user requests to a cheaper substitute model while billing for the advertised one. Detecting such partial substitution is challenging because honest providers also alter the output distribution through undocumented decoding and serving choices, such as temperature scaling, sampling truncation, repetition and presence penalties, and default system prompts, forcing an audit to test against a composite null of legitimate configurations rather than a single reference. Our key insight is that these legitimate variations primarily shift response typicality across the entire batch, whereas partial substitution injects individual responses that remain anomalous under the claimed model. Building on this, we introduce API-TAIL, a typicality audit that first absorbs batch-level shifts by aligning a single effective temperature to center standardized surprisal scores across the audited batch, and then flags the endpoint if the number of remaining tail responses exceeds a threshold calibrated across legitimate configurations. Evaluated on real-world commercial APIs, API-TAIL reliably controls false alarms across diverse honest providers while detecting even low-rate partial substitution with a small query budget, substantially outperforming existing rank- and MMD-based audits that lose detection power under the same composite calibration.

items.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.

items.title: Applying artificial intelligence to support cardiovascular risk prediction in resource-constrained settings: qualitative insights from Indonesian doctors
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk assessment underpins preventive care. Although machine learning models often outperform traditional risk prediction methods, adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinical decision support (CDS) tools remains limited, especially in resource-constrained settings. This study explored the sociotechnical context of CVD risk assessment in resource-constrained settings and identified potential applications for AI-based CDS. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 27 Indonesian doctors, including general practitioners and cardiologists. Interviews examined clinical decision-making processes, challenges associated with resource constraints, and potential use cases for AI-based CDS. Data were analyzed using a deductive thematic approach informed by the SEIPS (Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety) framework. Doctors reported managing high patient volumes, relying on paper-based medical records, and making largely subjective decisions due to limited access to confirmatory investigations and specialist support. Acute coronary syndrome resulting from atherosclerosis was identified as the most common and important clinical problem. Participants highlighted atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk assessment as a promising application for AI-based CDS because it uses widely available clinical information and can support preventive care decisions. Implementation of AI-based CDS should be guided by local clinical needs and sociotechnical context. Further research is needed to evaluate effects on clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.

items.title: ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection
items.abstract: Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Drone Patrol Implementation in Relation to Perceived Traffic Violation Reduction in Surabaya
items.abstract: Purpose - This study investigated the relationships of artificial intelligence (AI) utilization and drone patrol implementation with perceived traffic violation reduction in Surabaya, Indonesia. Design/methods/approach – A quantitative explanatory survey was analyzed using multiple linear regression in SPSS 25. The reported analyses contained 77 questionnaire records from personnel associated with the Surabaya City Police Traffic Unit. Findings – AI utilization (B = 0.424, β = 0.450, p < 0.001) and drone patrol implementation (B = 0.280, β = 0.334, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perceived traffic violation reduction. The model was significant, F(2, 74) = 36.065, p < 0.001, with R² = 0.494. Research implications/limitations – The results identify associations among respondents’ assessments, not observed changes in recorded violations. Operational evaluation should combine survey evidence with documented enforcement and road-safety outcomes. Originality/value – The study considers intelligent monitoring and mobile aerial patrols together in a specific urban policing setting while distinguishing perceived benefits from demonstrated causal effectiveness.

items.title: As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does
items.abstract: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.

items.title: Association Between Repetitive Movement Exposure and Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Symptoms Among Office Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Purpose: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) symptoms are an occupational health concern among office workers who perform repetitive hand and wrist movements during computer-based activities. This study aimed to examine the association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptoms among office workers at PT Karya Bintang Mandiri. Materials and Methods: This analytical cross-sectional study involved 164 office workers recruited using purposive sampling. Repetitive movement exposure was assessed using the Occupational Repetitive Actions (OCRA) Checklist, while CTS symptoms were evaluated using the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTQ). Descriptive statistics and the Pearson Chi-Square test were used to examine the association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptoms. Result: Moderate repetitive movement exposure was observed in 83 participants (50.6%), followed by high exposure in 42 (25.6%) and low exposure in 39 (23.8%). Regarding CTS symptoms, 62 participants (37.8%) reported no symptoms, 68 (41.5%) reported mild symptoms, 32 (19.5%) reported moderate symptoms, and 2 (1.2%) reported severe symptoms. The Pearson Chi-Square test indicated a significant association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptom categories, χ²(6) = 35.06, p < 0.001. In a supplementary dichotomized analysis, the prevalence of moderate-to-severe CTS symptoms was 47.6% (20/42) among workers with high exposure and 11.5% (14/122) among workers with low-to-moderate exposure (prevalence ratio [PR] = 4.15; 95% CI: 2.31–7.46). Conclusion: Repetitive movement exposure was associated with CTS symptom categories among office workers at PT Karya Bintang Mandiri. These findings support the importance of ergonomic risk assessment and preventive measures in office environments. Further studies using longitudinal designs and clinical diagnostic assessments are warranted.

items.title: ASTRA: An Autonomous Framework for Physics-Validated Analysis and Hypothesis Generation in Astrophysics
items.abstract: Abstract We present ASTRA, an autonomous framework for physics-validated analysis and hypothesis generation in astrophysics without per-step human intervention. It integrates dimensional analysis, structural causal models, Bayesian evidence computation, and multi-wavelength data fusion in a single automated workflow. Five test cases on real observational data recover known results: Herschel filament scaling, Chandra Deep Field South cross-matching, SDSS galaxy correlations, Gaia causal inference, and Bayesian virial model selection. A sixth case runs unsupervised on synthetic galaxy data: the main sequence and mass–metallicity relation are recovered, and the outlier detector, with a false-discovery-rate threshold and no contamination parameter, recovers the blind injected fraction on ten sealed datasets (purity >0.99) and flags nothing on the 3,000-galaxy sample. A knowledge-isolation ablation shows pattern detection and physical validation are invariant to removal of domain knowledge, which affects only interpretation. In a direct comparison, agentic-LLM and pure-ML baselines match the statistical fitting but not the physics-validation stage: they rarely derive the equilibrium benchmark, split evenly on the physical verdict, and adopt a supplied erroneous benchmark in all six trap runs; an astrophysics-specific fine-tuned model completes zero of six runs. On live SDSS DR16 data it flags 197 of 4,999 galaxies at a data-determined threshold, ranked extremes classifiable from withheld spectroscopy. These are recovery validations and capability demonstrations rather than discoveries, with hypothesis generation demonstrated qualitatively.

items.title: AudioRSI: Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

items.title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
items.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

items.title: AutoRSE: Evaluating LLM Agents as Recommendation Engineers for Self-Evolving Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Recommender Systems Engineer Agents (RSE-Agents), which use LLM-based agents to autonomously improve recommendation algorithms, are emerging as a promising paradigm. However, their capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood due to the lack of a unified, standardized evaluation framework and systematic trajectory-level analysis. To address this gap, we introduce AutoRSE, an evaluation framework spanning six representative industrial-grade recommendation tasks, and conduct a large-scale empirical study of three frontier LLMs across three widely used agent harnesses. Our results show that RSE-Agents consistently enhance the performance of backbones on five of the six tasks, with an average relative improvement of 16.1%, indicating that they can already autonomously improve recommendation performance. However, trajectory-level analysis also reveals that current RSE-Agents function primarily as engineering optimizers rather than algorithmic improvers: their gains are largely driven by hyperparameter tuning, training strategies, and model ensembling, while genuine algorithmic innovations are rare. Since the largest gains in recommender systems often stem from algorithmic advances, this behavior underscores a fundamental limitation of current RSE-Agents. To probe this limitation, we perform idea-injection experiments and show that agents equipped with innovative ideas from frontier research or human experts achieve substantially larger improvements than those relying on self-generated ideas. These results suggest that idea generation is a central bottleneck of current RSE-Agents, highlights a key direction for the future recommendation system research. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/Ray-Tiann/AutoRSE.

items.title: Balancing Cultural Preservation and Design: A Study on the Generative Artificial Intelligence-Empowered Framework for the Sustainable Design of Intangible Cultural Heritage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is a form of AI technology that can automatically generate new content, such as text, images, and audio, based on prompts. This study explores the opportunities and structural challenges of using Gen-AI to promote sustainable design in the field of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) from the perspectives of ICH designers and relevant experts. The research employed a variety of methods, including interviews (n= 40), grounded theory, the Delphi method (n = 20), exploratory factor analysis (n = 312), confirmatory factor analysis (n = 324), and expert interviews (n = 10). The study evaluated deep-seated issues arising from Gen-AI’s intervention in ICH design practices, such as cultural subjectivity, knowledge, power relations, and value circulation, through the lenses of Cultural Ecology, Extraction of Intangible Cultural Heritage Genes, Sustainable Communication, Technology Generation, and Human–Machine Collaborative Design. The results suggest that Gen-AI’s empowerment involves a tension between technological generative capabilities and cultural accuracy, as well as systemic-level transformations such as balancing communication efficiency with cultural depth and human–machine collaboration, and re-configuring the designer’s role.

items.title: BenchMeUp: Building Software Engineering Benchmarks from Natural-Language Specifications
items.abstract: Software-engineering research relies on benchmarks that evaluate new techniques on a set of problem instances. Unfortunately, manually constructing benchmarks is labor-intensive, as researchers must find suitable instances, prepare execution environments, establish expected outcomes, and validate correctness. This paper presents BenchMeUp, an approach for automatically creating software-engineering benchmarks from natural-language specifications. Given a specification defining the desired instances, data sources, and evaluation procedures, BenchMeUp generates search rules and a construction plan, invokes parallel LLM agents that identify candidate instances and construct executable instances, validates the results in fresh execution environments, and packages the instances behind a unified command-line interface. We evaluate the approach on four tasks: program repair, issue reproduction, compiler autotuning, and fixing static-analysis warnings. Targeting 50 instances per task (200 in total), BenchMeUp constructs 198 instances, of which 196 (99\%) are successfully packaged. Search and construction take 36 minutes and \$0.79 per instance, on average. Evaluating eight existing techniques on the generated benchmarks, we find that 189 of 196 packaged instances (96\%) support end-to-end evaluation, allowing users to study the effectiveness of the techniques. Checking every constructed instance against its source, the specification, and its expected outcome, we find that 180 of 198 (91\%) meet all criteria, compared with 10 of 200 instances delivered by Codex (general-purpose coding agent). Overall, we show that LLM-based agents can automate benchmark construction across diverse software-engineering tasks and produce executable instances that existing techniques can use, while validity beyond execution still needs to be checked.

items.title: Beyond Knowledge Transfer: the Multi-Faceted Role of Islamic Religious Education Teachers in Catalyzing Student Motivation
items.abstract: Students’ learning motivation is an important factor in effective learning, while Islamic Religious Education teachers have a strategic role in fostering motivation through pedagogical, motivational, and exemplary practices. This study aims to describe the planning and implementation of Islamic Religious Education teachers’ efforts to enhance students’ learning motivation and to analyze their outcomes in terms of student engagement, subject comprehension, religious attitudes, and character development. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design conducted at MTs Wahid Hasyim Dau Malang. The research subjects and data sources included 2 (two) Islamic Religious Education teachers, and 2 (two) administrative staff, and a class of students. Data were collected through observations, interviews, and documentation, and were analyzed using the Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña model through data condensation, data presentation, and conclusion drawing and verification, with data validity strengthened through cross-checking across sources and techniques. The findings show that teachers enhance learning motivation through systematic instructional planning, including the preparation of teaching modules, engaging learning activities, comprehensive assessment strategies, and adaptation of teaching methods to students’ characteristics. During implementation, teachers create a positive learning atmosphere through educational games, quizzes, discussions, question-and-answer sessions, group work, rewards, contextualization of learning materials, and regular content reviews. These efforts contribute to increased student participation, improved understanding of Islamic Religious Education materials, and the development of religious attitudes and character. The study recommends that teachers maintain varied and adaptive instructional strategies while strengthening students’ intrinsic motivation through meaningful learning experiences, positive reinforcement, role modeling, and collaboration between schools and parents.

items.title: Beyond the Evidence Coherence Trap: Agent-Driven Evidence Selection for Temporally Disordered Fake News Detection
items.abstract: Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. DelSA outperforms existing methods on ChronoFake, while remaining competitive on PolitiFact and GossipCop.

items.title: Bibliometric analysis of aviation unsafe event research: from reactive response to intelligent prediction
items.abstract: Purpose The post-pandemic recovery of global air transport and rapid developments in artificial intelligence are shifting aviation safety management from reactive accident investigation to proactive risk prediction. To examine how this trend is reflected in recent literature, this study aims to conduct a bibliometric analysis of aviation unsafe event research published between 2020 and 2025. Design/methodology/approach Based on 512 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, the authors use Bibliometrix and VOSviewer to construct keyword co-occurrence and co-citation networks. Findings The results show a rapid increase in research output following a temporary decline in 2022, reflecting the field’s resilience and growing attention to post-pandemic safety challenges. Thematic evolution analysis identifies a clear departure from traditional system-level investigations. This field increasingly prioritizes mining valuable information from flight data and unstructured safety reports using machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing. Current studies largely revolve around anomaly detection under complex meteorological conditions, causal inference using Bayesian networks and the application of large language models for safety text analysis. Originality/value These findings suggest that data-driven approaches have established themselves in aviation unsafe event research. Future studies should focus on addressing the interpretability of deep learning models and optimizing human–machine collaboration in safety-critical systems.

items.title: Biomedical Self-Supervised Learning using Sequential and Action-Conditioned Prediction: A Proof of Concept in Histopathology
items.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models for biomedical imaging are typically trained with non-sequential objectives that encourage invariance between augmented crops or predict missing content within a limited spatial resolution or range. This paradigm can be limiting for biomedical images, where diagnostically relevant structure often depends on relationships across widely different spatial extents and resolutions. We investigate sequential, action-conditioned prediction as an alternative self-supervised pretraining objective for biomedical imaging. As a proof of concept, we adapt seq-JEPA, originally developed for natural images, to 256 × 256 px histopathology images by extending its action space with zoom, and introduce seq-JEPA-dense, which predicts the next representation for every step in the sequence. Under the same per-crop augmentation distribution and with one run per method, seq-JEPA-dense improved tissue classification accuracy in the aggregated linear-probe evaluation from 88.3% to 91.9%, narrowing the gap to SimCLR, which achieved 93.3%. Both sequential variants recover a held-out crop from the preceding crops and the relative action leading to it at roughly twice the chance rate within the same image, indicating that the prediction depends on the action; whether position, zoom, or both drive this remains to be isolated. These results provide proof-of-concept evidence that sequential, action-conditioned self-supervision can be adapted to histopathology by extending its action space with zoom, yielding representations that approach a contrastive baseline, a first step toward its investigation as a self-supervised approach for extended biomedical images such as whole-slide images.

items.title: Bioprinting in Orthodontics: From Tissue Engineering to Personalized Regenerative Medicine
items.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting has emerged as an enabling technology in regenerative medicine with the potential to redefine the future of orthodontic treatment. By integrating living cells, biomaterials, and bioactive molecules through layer-by-layer fabrication, bioprinting enables the development of patient-specific constructs that closely replicate native craniofacial tissues. In orthodontics, this technology offers potential solutions for challenges such as alveolar bone deficiency, periodontal tissue loss, root resorption, craniofacial defects, and compromised tissue healing following orthodontic interventions. Recent advances in stem cell biology, bioactive hydrogels, tissue engineering, growth factor delivery, and digital manufacturing have expanded the scope of regenerative orthodontics beyond conventional biomechanical tooth movement. The incorporation of artificial intelligence, computer-aided design, cone-beam computed tomography, and additive manufacturing further supports precision treatment planning and customized regenerative therapies. Despite encouraging experimental outcomes, routine clinical implementation remains limited by challenges related to vascularization, scaffold maturation, manufacturing standardization, regulatory approval, long-term safety, and economic feasibility. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration among orthodontists, bioengineers, material scientists, and regulatory authorities is essential to translate laboratory innovations into predictable clinical applications. This article reviews the biological principles, technological advancements, clinical applications, translational challenges, and future perspectives of bioprinting, highlighting current evidence, existing limitations, and research priorities toward clinical translation.

items.title: Blockchain for space cybersecurity
items.abstract: Space infrastructure underpins modern civilisation but remains vulnerable because satellite communications, telemetry, and command systems rely heavily on centralised security architectures. As space becomes increasingly congested, contested, and commercialised, these architectures face growing threats from nation-state adversaries, cybercriminals, and supply chain compromise. This chapter examines blockchain technology as a structural countermeasure, highlighting how decentralisation, immutability, transparency, auditability, and trustless authentication address critical vulnerabilities across ground, space, user, cloud, communication, and supply chain segments. A permissioned consortium blockchain model is proposed to balance resilience, operational confidentiality, and national sovereignty requirements. The chapter explores blockchain-enabled applications including tamper-evident audit trails, decentralised identity and access management, distributed threat detection, smart contract governance, space situational awareness, autonomous satellite operations, and secure inter-satellite communications. It also analyses deployment challenges and future research directions involving post-quantum cryptography, Zero Trust Architecture, AI-enhanced smart contracts, and cislunar blockchain ecosystems for resilient and trustworthy next-generation space cybersecurity frameworks worldwide.

items.title: Body mass index modifies the noise-hypertension link: a cross-sectional study in automobile workers
items.abstract: Background Occupational noise is a pervasive occupational hazard. While it is a well-established cause of hearing loss, only a few studies have suggested a potential association with cardiovascular diseases, and the evidence remains limited. Furthermore, individual susceptibility varies substantially, and metabolic characteristics, such as body mass index (BMI), may play a modifying role. Objective To systematically examine the effect of BMI modification on occupational noise exposure duration and hypertension risk. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among workers at an automobile manufacturing plant. Demographics, occupational history, and medical examinations were collected. Modified Poisson regression models were used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs). The modifying effect of continuous BMI was evaluated by incorporating an interaction term, with a sensitivity analysis performed using binary BMI classifications. Johnson-Neyman technique was used to determine the point at which the association was no longer statistically significant. Results There were 21.6% of participants with hypertension in this plant. Occupational noise exposure duration was positively associated with the risk of hypertension. The continuous BMI showed a significant negative interaction with noise exposure duration (PR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.979–0.995], P = 0.001). Specifically, at a BMI of 18.5 kg/m 2 , each additional year of noise exposure duration increased hypertension risk by 11.9% (PR = 1.119, 95% CI [1.047–1.196]); at a BMI of 24.0 kg/m 2 , this association was attenuated but remained significant (PR = 1.041, 95% CI [1.008–1.075]); and at a BMI of 28.0 kg/m 2 , no significant association was observed (PR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.956–1.019]). With Johnson–Neyman, the BMI value above which the estimated association was no longer statistically significant was identified at 27.02 kg/m 2 . In sensitivity analysis, treating BMI as a binary variable, the association between noise exposure duration and hypertension risk was attenuated and no longer statistically significant in overweight/obese individuals but remained significant in normal-weight individuals, and the negative interaction between noise exposure duration and BMI remained statistically significant (PR = 0.919, 95% CI [0.863–0.979], P = 0.010). Conclusions The association between occupational noise exposure duration and hypertension risk was modified by BMI in this cross-sectional study of automobile manufacturing workers. The association was more pronounced among normal-weight workers, whereas it was attenuated and no longer statistically significant at higher BMI levels. These findings suggest that BMI may be an important consideration in occupational health surveillance and hypertension risk assessment among noise-exposed workers, warranting further longitudinal investigation.

items.title: Bootstrap Stability and Learner Sensitivity in Bayesian Network Modeling of near Midair Collision Incidents Using Aviation Safety Narratives and Operational Data
items.abstract: Near midair collisions (NMACs) remain a complex aviation safety challenge shaped by operational conditions and human factors. Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) narratives provide useful information about communication, visual acquisition, workload, and other event circumstances, but relationships identified from voluntary reports may vary across analytical approaches and over time. This study examined 13,111 NMAC-related ASRS reports from 1988 to 2025 to identify stable report-level associations among operational conditions, encounter proximity, narrative topics, and reported evasive action. Across two Bayesian-network approaches and 500 paired bootstrap samples, traffic-pattern operations/training and tower communication/sequencing were the strongest variables directly associated with reported evasive action. Their recurrence was moderate rather than universal, however, and their inclusion changed under different relationship-selection thresholds. This indicates that the local structure around reported evasive action was sensitive to modeling decisions, even though the two variables consistently ranked as the leading response-adjacent candidates. Additional robustness checks preserved these two response parents in the full-data models while showing changes in the broader network structure. A temporal evaluation produced a different pattern. Models trained on reports from 1988 to 2019 and evaluated on reports from 2020 to 2025 instead identified airspace structure/radar-contact issues and final-approach/base-to-final conflicts as the response-adjacent variables. Because the narrative-topic features were derived from the full corpus, this analysis represents a temporal evaluation conditional on a fixed topic representation, rather than a fully independent validation of the complete modeling pipeline. The changed response parents therefore indicate temporal sensitivity but do not establish nonstationarity. The findings describe associations within voluntary safety reports and should not be interpreted as evidence of causality, collision risk, or operational warning performance. The study contributes a reproducible, systematically stress-tested framework for evaluating Bayesian-network findings in aviation safety narratives. It identifies communication, sequencing, visual acquisition, and traffic-pattern operations as priorities for expert review and prospective measurement while cautioning against treating relationships found in historical narratives as stable operational predictors.

items.title: Brain-Inspired AI in Industry, Infrastructure, and Innovation
items.abstract: The accelerating integration of brain-inspired artificial intelligence into industrial systems marks a transformative moment for sustainable engineering, directly advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 9 on Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure. This chapter provides a rigorous, engineering-oriented examination of how neuroscience principles, including spike-timing-dependent plasticity, predictive coding, hierarchical sensory processing, and lateral inhibition, are being systematically translated into industrial AI architectures with compelling real-world impact. Six interconnected domains are explored: cognitive robotics and human–machine collaboration using ACT-R-grounded spiking neural networks; digital twin-integrated predictive maintenance leveraging liquid state machines and event-driven spike encoding; energy-aware neuromorphic computing for sustainable manufacturing, achieving up to 10,000× power reduction over GPU-based systems; brain-inspired hierarchical decision systems and neuro-symbolic integration for explainable smart factory control; ethical workforce transition frameworks addressing automation’s socioeconomic implications; and six global innovation case studies spanning wind turbine health monitoring, electric vehicle battery assembly, smart city traffic optimization, and predictive water infrastructure management. Collectively, these applications demonstrate that brain-inspired AI is not merely a technical advancement but a principled pathway toward more resilient, equitable, and environmentally sustainable industrial systems aligned with international development goals.

items.title: Bridging Human–AI Interaction and Human–Robot Interaction: Shared Challenges, Converging Futures
items.abstract: This panel examines the growing convergence of human–AI interaction (HAI) and human–robot interaction (HRI) as intelligent systems become more autonomous, embodied, and embedded in everyday settings such as healthcare, education, homes, and workplaces. Although HAI and HRI have evolved as distinct fields, the panel argues that shared human factors concerns—such as trust, safety, autonomy, teamwork, situation awareness, evaluation, and responsible deployment—now require greater integration across both domains. Drawing on perspectives from leading researchers and doctoral students, the session explores how embodiment, motion, social cues, and system transparency shape human interaction with AI and robots. It also addresses methodological tensions, including laboratory versus field evaluation and short-term versus longitudinal study, while highlighting implications for ethics, training, and design. Overall, the panel aims to identify common challenges, foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, and outline a research roadmap for human-centered intelligent systems that improve performance, well-being, and quality of life across diverse contexts and sectors.

items.title: CaLLM: Continual Adaptation of LLMs via Non-Parametric Adapter Routing
items.abstract: Continual adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to evolving task distributions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting remains an open problem. Existing strategies often struggle to scale or lack a robust mechanism for zero-shot task-to-expert assignment. We introduce CaLLM, a framework that resolves these tensions by combining metric-based meta-learning with modular parameter isolation via lightweight adapters. First, CaLLM projects each input batch into a task-agnostic embedding space to find its nearest prototype. It then routes the batch to the specific adapter specialized for that data distribution. This formulation provides (i)~controllable cross-task interference by design, (ii)~constant computational complexity regardless of task count, (iii)~seamless integration of novel distributions through prototype expansion, and (iv)~regime agnosticism as the local routing decision enables a unified approach to both online and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that this routing mechanism discovers semantically coherent task groupings while facilitating constructive interference between similar tasks, and keeping overhead at a minimum. Across diverse and fine-grained continual learning benchmarks, CaLLM consistently outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods, establishing prototype-based modular routing as a principled and scalable approach to lifelong adaptation of LLMs.

items.title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.

items.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.
